strengths: Directly and convincingly challenges a widely cited prior conclusion (Yeh et al., 2022, 'first is better than last') with both theoretical and empirical evidence; the counterexample theorem (Appendix G) provides a clean argument that high gradient cancellation can improve influence estimates.

Extensive experimental scope: 4 models spanning 355M–7B parameters (RoBERTa-Large, Llama-3.2 1B, Qwen-2.5 1.5B, Mistral 7B), 8 GLUE datasets, 3 influence methods (TracIn, DataInf, Cosine), layer-wise groupings, and 10 random seeds per configuration — a rigorous and costly evaluation protocol.

Practical contribution via the Rank and Vote aggregation strategies, which consistently outperform standard mean aggregation (e.g., DataInf win rate rising to 0.84 on Mistral), demonstrating that aggregation across layers is an underexplored and impactful design choice.

The Noise Detection Rate (NDR) proxy metric is a useful practical tool for assessing influence methods without costly fine-tuning, and the paper is honest about its limitations (correlations of 0.5–0.7 rather than overstated claims).

Well-structured around clearly formulated research questions (RQ1–RQ4), with detailed appendices covering setup, per-model results, noise distributions, and the full proof, supporting reproducibility and transparency.
The analysis of noise concentration at both extremes of the influence distribution (Appendix I) explains why filtering fails on some models (e.g., Llama) and adds nuance beyond headline results.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to GLUE-style classification tasks with synthetic label-flipping noise (20%); no experiments with real-world noise, generative tasks, or instruction-tuned settings, which weakens the generality of the central claim about LLM influence estimation.

The theoretical contribution (Theorem 5.1) is a fairly simple existence/counterexample construction with restrictive assumptions (TracIn-only, scalar gradient analysis, dependence on a validation point); it refutes a general claim but does not provide a constructive alternative criterion.

Results on Llama-3.2 1B are largely negative (influence methods fall below the Random baseline), which limits the practical impact of the proposed layer and aggregation guidance; the paper acknowledges but does not fully explain this discrepancy.

Statistical rigor is uneven: significance is reported with Wilcoxon p < 0.1 over only 10 runs, which is a weak threshold; Vote aggregation also degrades performance for Cosine and on CoLA/QQP, so the 'consistently outperforms' claim is only partially supported.

The aggregation strategies (rank voting, positional voting) are simple heuristics with limited conceptual novelty, and the NDR/AUC proxy metrics show only moderate correlations (0.5–0.7) in many configurations, so their reliability as replacements for retraining-based evaluation is not yet established.
No explicit statement about code release, and the computational cost of the full protocol (many fine-tuning runs across 4 models × 8 datasets × 10 seeds) may hinder independent reproduction.

strengths: Extensive empirical scope: 4 models (RoBERTa-Large, Llama-3.2 1B, Qwen-2.5 1.5B, Mistral 7B), 8 GLUE datasets, 10 seeds per configuration, and a well-defined multi-stage evaluation pipeline, which gives the empirical claims reasonable statistical support.

The paper directly challenges a concrete, prior claim (Yeh et al., 2022) that embedding layers are best for influence estimation, and the layer-wise findings (middle attention layers outperforming embedding and classification-head layers for larger models) are potentially useful to practitioners using influence functions.
The proposed Rank/Vote aggregation methods and the NDR/AUC proxy metrics address a real practical problem (avoiding costly retraining-based evaluation of influence methods).
The paper is generally well organized around explicit research questions, and appendices provide substantial additional detail on setup, layer rankings, and noise distributions.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the core contributions. The aggregation strategies (Rank and Vote) are simple, well-known heuristics (rank aggregation and k-voting) applied to influence scores; NDR is essentially the fraction of known noisy samples in the filtered set, and AUC over the influence ranking is a standard measure (cf. Plessis et al., 2020). Neither requires substantial methodological innovation.

The theoretical contribution is weak. Theorem 5.1 is a contrived existence result: it posits two parameter vectors with C(ω) → ∞ and claims the existence of a single validation point x3 where the noisy–clean separation improves. The proof's key step ('such universal anti-alignment is impossible') is informal and hand-wavy, and the assumptions essentially encode the conclusion. This does not establish that the cancellation effect is 'unreliable' in any general sense; it only shows one adversarially constructed case, which is not surprising.

The central empirical claims are narrower than the framing suggests. The evaluation uses only synthetic label-flip noise on GLUE classification tasks with small subsampled datasets (4500 train samples), LoRA fine-tuning, and fixed 30% filtering. No natural/realistic noise, no generative tasks, and no other domains are tested, so the claim that 'first is not really better than last' may not generalize beyond this specific setup.

Mixed and partially negative results undermine practical significance: on Llama-3.2 1B, none of the influence-based configurations beat the uniform Random filtering baseline (Section 5.2, Figure 9), and Vote/Rank degrade performance on CoLA and QQP for several models. The paper does not provide a clear predictive account of when the proposed methods help versus hurt.

The proposed proxy metrics are not convincingly reliable: NDR/AUC correlations with final accuracy are mostly in the 0.5–0.7 range (Table 2), often not statistically significant, and the authors themselves conclude these are 'not consistently reliable.' A proxy that frequently fails to predict downstream performance offers limited value as an evaluation tool.

Statistical methodology is questionable in places: Wilcoxon tests with p < 0.1 and only 10 runs, and 'win rate' comparisons at a 75% threshold, are weak standards for the paired-comparison conclusions drawn.

Presentation issues: Figures 2 and 3 are dense, hard to parse box plots with many overlapping configurations; key quantitative results are deferred to appendices; and the main text often describes trends qualitatively ('outperform', 'comparable') without giving effect sizes.

Positioning is somewhat overstated: the paper presents itself as refuting Yeh et al. (2022), but that work used a different metric (expected prediction change for top-k opponents) and smaller models; differences in setup (e.g., compressed embeddings, frozen WE, LoRA) make the direct comparison 'first vs. last' less conclusive than claimed.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly scoped study that directly challenges an influential prior claim (Yeh et al., 2022) about layer choice in influence functions, with both empirical and theoretical support for the rebuttal.

Extensive experimental coverage: 4 models spanning 355M to 7B parameters (RoBERTa-Large, Llama-3.2 1B, Qwen-2.5 1.5B, Mistral 7B), 8 GLUE tasks, 3 influence functions, multiple layer groupings, and 10 seeds per configuration, with detailed appendix material (rankings, noise histograms, correlation analyses).

The proposed Rank and Vote aggregation strategies are simple, practically relevant, and show consistent gains for DataInf/TracIn (e.g., DataInf win rate rising to 0.84 on Mistral), establishing that aggregation is a real, previously overlooked factor.
The NDR/AUC proxy metrics address a genuine practical pain point (avoiding costly fine-tuning-based evaluation) and show strong correlations (0.8-0.9) under Vote aggregation.

Honest reporting of negative results, e.g., influence methods failing to beat the Random baseline on Llama-3.2, and noise concentrating at both extremes of the influence range, which adds credibility.

Reproducibility is reasonably supported: detailed pipeline description (Appendix A), hyperparameters, memory/batching analysis, and multiple statistical checks (Wilcoxon tests, win rates, Spearman correlations).
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is weak: Theorem 5.1 only asserts existence of a single validation point where including high-cancellation weights improves noisy/clean separation, which is a near-trivial existential statement; the proof even resorts to informal appeals ('typically share co-directional gradients'), and the authors' own remark concedes the reverse inequality also occurs, so the result neither rigorously refutes nor charitably characterizes the cancellation effect.

Evaluation scope is narrow: only synthetic 20% label flips on classification-style GLUE tasks (STS-B binarized, MNLI reduced to two classes) with small subsets (4500 train / 500 test); no real-world noise, no generative or instruction-tuning settings, limiting the generality of the headline claim for 'LLMs'.

Results are internally inconsistent with the paper's central message: on Llama-3.2 no configuration beats Random filtering, WE is best for TracIn on RoBERTa, and layer preferences vary by model and task. The 'middle layers are better' conclusion is more nuanced than the title and abstract suggest.
The Rank/Vote methods are straightforward Borda-count-style heuristics with modest novelty, and they actively hurt Cosine and some datasets (CoLA, QQP), so the claimed improvement is not universal.

Missing important baselines for the data-filtering task itself: no comparison against established noise-detection methods such as area-under-margin, self-influence, or loss-based filtering, making it hard to judge whether influence-based layer selection is competitive for noise removal in general.

NDR/AUC correlations under mean aggregation are only moderate (0.4-0.7) and some are not statistically significant; the claim that NDR is a 'reliable' proxy is somewhat stronger than the evidence, particularly for Rank aggregation where correlations collapse on Llama.

Evaluation by 'best test accuracy' over epochs and 10 seeds with a lenient Wilcoxon threshold (p < 0.1) is a generous protocol; some conclusions would benefit from stricter significance testing and more runs.

strengths: The paper directly challenges a well-known prior result (Yeh et al., 2022, 'First is better than last') with a combination of theoretical analysis and extensive empirical evidence, which is a meaningful contribution to the data attribution literature.

Very comprehensive experimental design: four models (RoBERTa-Large, Llama-3.2 1B, Qwen-2.5 1.5B, Mistral 7B), eight GLUE datasets, three influence functions plus two embedding-based variants, 10 random seeds, and rigorous statistical testing (Friedman, Wilcoxon), with pairwise win-rate and Pareto-front comparisons.

The proposed Rank and Vote aggregation strategies are simple but show consistent and statistically supported improvements over standard mean aggregation (e.g., DataInf win rate improving to 0.84 on Mistral), and the analysis of layer-group correlations (Appendix E/Fig. 13) provides good motivation for why aggregation matters.

The Noise Detection Rate (NDR) and AUC proxy metrics address a real practical pain point (avoiding expensive retraining-based evaluation of influence methods), and the paper is honest about their moderate correlation levels (0.5-0.7) and about which settings they are reliable in.

Findings are validated beyond the main setting: additional experiments on autoregressive datasets from Kwon et al. (2024) and more recent methods (EK-FAC/Kronfluence, RepSim, Outlier Gradient) support the layer-choice conclusions, and a practical recommendation (LoRA Value B modules) is consistently supported across models.
Reproducibility is taken seriously: open-sourced code, fixed seeds, determinism, documented hyperparameters, and a detailed experimental protocol in the appendix.
weaknesses: Generalizability of the central claims is weakened by the Llama-3.2 1B results, where influence-based filtering fails to outperform the Random baseline under mean aggregation (only partially rescued by Vote on specific modules); the title-level claim ('first is not really better than last') rests partly on settings where the influence signal itself is weak.

The theoretical contribution (Theorem 5.1) is a relatively weak existence/counterexample result, and the proof leans on an informal claim that parameter vectors 'typically share co-directional gradients on at least some validation points,' which is not made rigorous.

The empirical refutation of the cancellation effect uses a modified protocol (single checkpoint in evaluation mode rather than the original size-one batching over training), so the comparison to Yeh et al. (2022) is not a perfectly apples-to-apples refutation of their exact setting.

Scope is narrower than the framing suggests: the main experiments concern LoRA fine-tuning of classification heads on GLUE with synthetically injected label noise, with generative/autoregressive results relegated to the appendix; the paper's positioning around 'LLMs' somewhat overstates the setting.

Presentation and clarity issues: Table 7 (Appendix M) appears misreported or at least highly confusing (e.g., 'Full' with accuracy 1.20 ± 0.80, units unexplained), some figures (Figs. 3, 13) are hard to read, there are minor typos/inconsistencies (e.g., 'indetifying', Llama-3.2 cited via the Llama 2 report), and NDR's definition is spread across Sections 5.4 and Appendix A.

Novelty is moderate: the aggregation heuristics (rank/vote) are straightforward, and the middle-layer finding is acknowledged to be consistent with prior observations from the knowledge-editing literature (ROME/MEMIT); the paper is primarily a careful empirical study rather than a methodological advance.

The NDR/AUC proxy metrics achieve only moderate correlations in many configurations (0.4-0.7, sometimes non-significant), so their practical utility as reliable replacements for retraining-based evaluation is only partially demonstrated.

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant and underexplored question: which model layers (and which aggregation strategies) should be used for influence-function-based data attribution in LLMs, directly challenging the influential 'first is better than last' conclusion of Yeh et al. (2022).

Empirically thorough: four models spanning 355M–7B parameters (RoBERTa-Large, Llama-3.2 1B, Qwen-2.5 1.5B, Mistral 7B), eight GLUE datasets, three influence methods plus embedding-specific variants, 10 random seeds, and statistical significance testing (Friedman, Wilcoxon), with full per-configuration results in the appendix.

Provides both empirical (Spearman correlations between cancellation metric C and downstream accuracy) and theoretical (a counterexample-style theorem, Appendix G) evidence that the cancellation effect is an unreliable layer-selection criterion.

The Rank and Vote aggregation strategies are simple, well-motivated (mitigating score compensation/dominance across layers), and show consistent gains over mean aggregation in several settings (e.g., DataInf win rate rising to 0.84 on Mistral).

The proposed proxy metrics (Noise Detection Rate and AUC) address a real cost problem — avoiding expensive retraining-based evaluation of influence methods — and correlations of 0.8–0.9 under Vote aggregation are encouraging.
Reproducibility is well supported: open-sourced code, fixed seeds, determinism settings, and a detailed experimental protocol (Appendix A), including compute/memory optimization details.
Additional validation on autoregressive datasets (Appendix J) with newer methods (EKFAC, RepSim, Outlier Gradient) extends the scope beyond synthetic GLUE noise.
weaknesses: Mixed and sometimes negative headline results undermine the central narrative: for Llama-3.2 1B, none of the influence configurations beat the Random removal baseline in the main experiments, and the 'best layer' varies substantially across model-dataset-method combinations (RoBERTa peaks in later layers). This weakens the paper's actionable takeaway that 'middle layers are better' and makes the title's claim feel overgeneralized relative to the evidence.

The theoretical contribution (Theorem 5.1) is thin: it is essentially an existence argument relying on an assumption of universal gradient anti-alignment being 'impossible,' with informal justification ('typically share co-directional gradients'). It demonstrates a counterexample to Yeh et al. (2022) but does not establish any positive characterization of when/why certain layers are better.

Novelty of the aggregation methods is modest: rank-based and Borda-like positional voting schemes are standard techniques, applied here rather than invented; the theoretical grounding for why they help in this specific setting is largely absent (only post-hoc correlation analysis motivates them).

Proxy metric (NDR/AUC) correlations are only moderate (0.5–0.7) in many configurations, with several non-significant results, so the claim that these are 'reliable indicators' of downstream performance is stronger than the evidence; the Vote-aggregation correlation boost is confounded with the aggregation gains themselves.

Evaluation scope is narrow: only synthetic 20% uniform label-flip noise on classification-style GLUE tasks (with STS-B binarized and MNLI binarized), LoRA fine-tuning only, and relatively small fine-tuning sets (up to 4500 samples). Generalization to realistic noise types, larger-scale training, and generation tasks is asserted but not demonstrated.

The Vote method introduces a hyperparameter k whose optimal value interacts with the noise level ('remains an open question'), and k=30 is chosen somewhat ad hoc for the main experiments; Cosine degrades under Vote/Rank, so the aggregation contribution is method-dependent rather than uniform.

Several presentation issues reduce polish: typos ('indetifying'), dense and hard-to-parse result tables (Tables 4–6), inconsistent notation in Eq. 9/10, and some claims supported only in sprawling appendix material, making the main-paper argumentation harder to follow.

Significance/impact is limited: the paper is primarily a careful negative/empirical re-evaluation plus simple heuristic aggregation and proxy metrics; it does not propose a new influence estimation technique, and its findings are conditional on the specific benchmark setup.

strengths: Timely and well-motivated study that directly challenges an established claim (Yeh et al., 2022) about layer choice in language data influence estimation, with both empirical evidence and a theoretical counterexample (Theorem 5.1 / Appendix G).

Comprehensive experimental scope: four models spanning 355M–7B parameters (RoBERTa-Large, Llama-3.2 1B, Qwen-2.5 1.5B, Mistral 7B), eight GLUE datasets, 10 seeds, three influence functions, and multiple aggregation strategies, with appropriate statistical testing (Friedman, Wilcoxon) and careful pairwise comparison / Pareto-front analysis.

Practically useful contributions beyond the critique: the Rank and Vote aggregation schemes are simple, well-motivated by the observed layer compensation patterns (Appendix D/E), and yield consistent, statistically significant improvements over mean aggregation (e.g., DataInf win rate rising to 0.84 on Mistral; rescuing CL-layer configurations).

The Noise Detection Rate (NDR) proxy metric is a valuable practical contribution, potentially saving costly retraining-based evaluation, and the paper is commendably honest about its limitations (correlations of 0.5–0.7 for Mean aggregation, and the failure of influence methods to beat Random on Llama-3.2 1B, which is analyzed rather than hidden).

Strong reproducibility: open-sourced code, fixed seeds, determinism enabled, detailed appendix covering hyperparameters, batching/memory optimizations, LoRA module analysis, autoregressive dataset validation (Appendix J), and the Vote-k sensitivity study (Appendix L).
weaknesses: The main experiments rely on synthetic label noise (20% uniform label flipping) on GLUE classification tasks. Conclusions about layer effectiveness and cancellation may not transfer to realistic, structured, or distribution-shift noise, and the setup involves classification-head fine-tuning of decoder LLMs rather than the generative settings where influence functions are most often deployed (the autoregressive validation in Appendix J partially but only partially mitigates this).

Generality of the central claim is limited: the 'best' layers are model-, task-, and method-specific (e.g., later layers for RoBERTa, early/middle for Mistral, and complete failure to beat Random on Llama-3.2 1B under Mean aggregation). The practical guidance is therefore somewhat contingent, and the headline 'middle layers are better' is an oversimplification of the actual findings.

The Vote method introduces a hyperparameter k, and the reported results use knowledge gained from ground-truth noise analysis (e.g., k=30 chosen based on NDR curves that require knowing the flipped labels). The dependence of recommendations on oracle-labeled noise weakens the claimed utility of NDR and Vote as deployable tools.

The theoretical contribution is a fairly simple constructive existence result (a counterexample showing high-cancellation weights can improve separation); it establishes non-generality of Yeh et al.'s claim but provides limited insight into when or why.

Proxy-metric correlations (NDR/AUC vs. downstream accuracy) are only moderate for most configurations (0.4–0.7), so the claim that these metrics 'exhibit strong predictive capability' is stronger than the evidence; NDR also fundamentally requires ground-truth noise labels, limiting its real-world applicability.

Presentation issues: several typos ('indetifying', 'bettser', 'TracInf'), inconsistent citation formatting, and the headline figure 3 is dense and hard to parse; some key conclusions (e.g., layer rankings) are pushed to appendices.
